Wall Street’s “fear gauges” just had their biggest day in years. So what normally happens next?

The VIX jumped 69.7% to 28.17 Thursday, its biggest one-day gain since December 2024 and second-largest since the February 2018 “Volmageddon,” per Cboe. It was also its highest close since March 30.

The VVIX (the VIX of the VIX) rose 49.3% to 134.99, its biggest one-day gain since February 2007 and its biggest point gain since Volmageddon. So traders weren’t just hedging against further stock declines, they were scrambling to hedge volatility itself.

What history says (calculations from Cboe data):
▪️ VIX up 60%+ in a day (5 prior cases since 1990): S&P 500 higher a month later all 5 times
▪️ VIX up 40%+ (24 cases): higher a month later 18 times, and a year later 22 times, by an average of almost 19%
▪️ VIX up 40%+ and VVIX up 30%+ the same day (6 cases since 2007): higher a month later every time, but a year later only 4 of 6, averaging about 4%

Big caveat with the small sample sizes, and note it can be just the start of something much bigger, like February 2020, when the S&P was down 24% a month later. 

Getting more granular, spikes from a calm base like this one have had weaker three-month follow-through. And the closest match for both gauges, February 27, 2007, saw the S&P slightly lower a year later.

Why I keep a potential 100× outcome on the table for HydroGraph and have made it my biggest bet ever: exceptional margins combined with production capacity that can be replicated.

The attached table puts numbers behind that possibility.

At an assumed selling price of US$250/kg, selling 10,000 tonnes annually would generate US$2.5 BILLION in revenue. US$250/kg is the minimum price, in most cases it will be much higher.

• 5,000 tonnes at P/E 30 → C$67.92/share. • 10,000 tonnes at P/E 30 → C$135.84/share. • 20,000 tonnes at P/E 40 → C$362.25/share.

These are conditional future valuations, not price targets. The assumptions are shown in the table.

Its modular Hyperion reactors can be built in months. If commercial margins hold and customers place repeat orders, profits could help fund additional reactors and eventually additional sites.

That creates a compelling possibility: growing volumes, strong earnings and expansion increasingly funded internally.

The opportunity spans coatings, polymers, concrete and defense. Successful adoption across several of those markets could support a business far larger than the first Texas facility.

I'm happy to be partnering with @mezzanine_fi to bring a bit of attention to their protocol, because I think they're trying something interesting here

In simple terms, most DeFi vaults treat everyone the same. Everyone earns the same yield, and if something goes wrong everyone takes the same hit.

Mezzanine splits each vault into two sides:

Junior: which takes any losses first if the strategy loses money, in return for a higher yield for taking the risk

Senior: which earns a smaller share of the yield but only takes a loss once Junior has been wiped out, so it has some added downside coverage

Losses can still happen of course, but this allows depositors to have more customization in their risk/reward level while not changing the underlying strategy of the vault

My current strategy is just to use the Senior pool and take the modest (but still good) yield, mostly b/c i'm at a point where I don't want or need to be taking on additional risks with my stables and am content with 8-9% yield.

Where does the yield come from? Always the right question to ask. The yield in their first vault comes from real-world loans, home equity and car loans made through Figure (via Hastra) which is then looped to boost it.

The full chain is: people take out home or car loans through Figure, a big US fintech company that makes loans. Hastra brings Figure's loan interest into DeFi and turns the interest into tokens, Mezzanine borrows against those tokens on Morpho and Kamino to earn more, and then splits the result between Senior and Junior.

Right now the app shows 8.5% APY for Senior and 20.7% for Junior, though that moves week to week

As always NFA/DYOR, but imo it's worth checking out.

- Are you spending more than you make?

- What % of your net worth is your largest position? Is it too big?

This is not a market call. I have no idea what the market will do. This is about good financial hygiene so you don’t panic and do something stupid.

Nasdaq-100 forward returns after one-day drops of 6.25% or more, like today’s (NDX, Jan 1985 to Nov 2026, n=33 days).

Takeaways:

➤ 21 days later: average +5.2% vs +1.3% for any day. Index higher in 64% of cases vs 63%.

➤ 63 days later: average +4.9% vs +4.1% for any day. Index higher in 64% of cases vs 69%. By 3 months the edge is mostly gone.

➤ Further losses common: NDX fell another 10% or more within 63 days in 21 of 33 cases.

➤ In 1987 and 2020 a fast policy backstop ended the forced selling within two weeks. In 2000–01 and 2008 earnings and credit losses that policy couldn’t fix kept the index falling for months.

Today’s trigger was the midterms. Texas elected Hinojosa as governor on a promise to freeze data center permits, and voters elsewhere passed restrictions in 40 of 41 local data center ballot measures.

The obvious comparison is 2000. But the 2000 crash came from collapsing demand, while this comes from expected policy changes, and expectations can reverse.

The closest precedent is April 2025: NDX fell 6.1% on tariffs, Trump hit pause three sessions later, and NDX was up 30.5% after 63 days. Then one person caused the shock and could reverse it. Here expectations depend on a new governor and Congress, so a V-reversal is harder.

There is a flipside. The same Democratic wave that threatens the AI buildout also limits Trump’s room to escalate in Iran. A deal is barely priced. Lower oil would mean a less hawkish Fed, and lower rates help long-duration tech the most.

Citrini's "State of the Themes" article kinda strengthens the Onchain/Decentralized AI thesis
 
The article argued that the AI infra/semis trades are ending because Neoclouds/Hyperscalers CAPEX is hitting ~$1T while AI eco ARR is only $200B and the huge gap won't be filled any time soon. Plus, financing constraints, construction delays and model price competition add pressure to the trade
 
That creates an interesting setup for projects helping operators monetize existing capacity and buyers access cheaper compute.
 
This is where Onchain/Decentralized AI gets interesting
 
1. Turning idle/crowdsourced GPUs into revenue
 
GPU marketplaces like @lium_io help operators rent out unused capacity, connecting existing hardware with paying customers.
 
For data centers and smaller operators, better utilization means more revenue from assets they’ve already paid for. Buyers get more options and competitive pricing (e.g. rent idle B200s on @lium_io for $4.25/hr).
 
As financing gets tighter, making existing hardware earn more becomes increasingly valuable.
 
2. Building markets for surplus/excess inference
 
Inference Providers and AI gateways have inference capacity they can sell. Some are expirables because they run subsidy campaigns but they couldn't get users to fully use them.
 
@AskSurplus connects these participants through an inference marketplace, routing requests across discounted supply. Selected offers carry discounts of 50–99% relative to listed API prices.
 
This creates a way for sellers to monetize unused allocations and buyers to reduce their inference bills.
 
Onchain settlement and tokenized credits add building blocks for developers to create new markets, routing tools and products around that supply.
 
3. Bootstrapping inference networks with existing GPUs
 
Decentralized AI crowdsources idle GPUs across the world.
 
Token emissions are used to pay for compute & inference instead of debt & equity financing huge CAPEX for data center buildouts.
 
Teams like @engyai and @dphnAI are already proving that it's possible to host top open-weight models on a hybrid/fully decentralized network that's fast, reliable, and cheap for users.
 
The opportunity is to turn fragmented hardware into useful, competitively priced inference.
 
The economics become stronger as paying customer demand grows enough to support suppliers with progressively smaller subsidies.
 
4. Expanding access to GPU financing
 
@USDai_Official connects onchain capital with operators financing GPU infrastructure.
 
That gives smaller operators another route to funding hardware purchases and deployments, with loans secured by GPUs and supported by their cash flows.
 
As traditional financing becomes more selective, access to additional capital sources could become increasingly valuable.
 
5. Making inference access a tradable asset
 
Pilots of inference tokenization are happening onchain first
 
@AskVenice tokenized its platform credits into "DIEM", people are buying & selling inference like a commodity and builders are building on top of it, creating venues where users can speculate & earn from their credits.
 
This creates the market for future inference access. Users can acquire capacity, trade the token representing that access, and earn revenue from it (if they don't use it).
 
Other teams are experimenting with similar models, creating more ways to price, distribute and monetize inference.
 
For tokens, this creates a link with extraneous demand outside of crypto. The more people use the platform, the more valuable the credits, the more valuable the token.
 
The investment case gets stronger when usage translates into value for token holders
 
The best part is that this sector is growing fast and teams are starting to align interest with token holders through buybacks & burn, revenue distribution, and more utilities.
 
Onchain/Decentralized AI provides the opportunities for better GPU utilization, cheaper inference, new financing channels and tradable access to compute/inference.
 
All real economic problems that crypto teams are building products around them.
 
2025-26 is the year of AI infra/semiconductors
 
2027 will be the year of Onchain/Decentralized AI

That creates an interesting setup for projects helping operators monetize existing capacity and buyers access cheaper compute.
 
This is where Onchain/Decentralized AI gets interesting
 
1. Turning idle/crowdsourced GPUs into revenue
 
GPU marketplaces like @lium_io help operators rent out unused capacity, connecting existing hardware with paying customers.
 
For data centers and smaller operators, better utilization means more revenue from assets they’ve already paid for. Buyers get more options and competitive pricing (e.g. rent idle B200s on @lium_io for $4.25/hr).
 
As financing gets tighter, making existing hardware earn more becomes increasingly valuable.
 
2. Building markets for surplus/excess inference
 
Inference Providers and AI gateways have inference capacity they can sell. Some are expirables because they run subsidy campaigns but they couldn't get users to fully use them.
 
@AskSurplus connects these participants through an inference marketplace, routing requests across discounted supply. Selected offers carry discounts of 50–99% relative to listed API prices.
 
This creates a way for sellers to monetize unused allocations and buyers to reduce their inference bills.
 
Onchain settlement and tokenized credits add building blocks for developers to create new markets, routing tools and products around that supply.
 
3. Bootstrapping inference networks with existing GPUs
 
Decentralized AI crowdsources idle GPUs across the world.
 
Token emissions are used to pay for compute & inference instead of debt & equity financing huge CAPEX for data center buildouts.
 
Teams like @engyai and @dphnAI are already proving that it's possible to host top open-weight models on a hybrid/fully decentralized network that's fast, reliable, and cheap for users.
 
The opportunity is to turn fragmented hardware into useful, competitively priced inference.
 
The economics become stronger as paying customer demand grows enough to support suppliers with progressively smaller subsidies.
 
4. Expanding access to GPU financing
 
@USDai_Official connects onchain capital with operators financing GPU infrastructure.
 
That gives smaller operators another route to funding hardware purchases and deployments, with loans secured by GPUs and supported by their cash flows.
 
As traditional financing becomes more selective, access to additional capital sources could become increasingly valuable.
 
5. Making inference access a tradable asset
 
Pilots of inference tokenization are happening onchain first
 
@AskVenice tokenized its platform credits into "DIEM", people are buying & selling inference like a commodity and builders are building on top of it, creating venues where users can speculate & earn from their credits.
 
This creates the market for future inference access. Users can acquire capacity, trade the token representing that access, and earn revenue from it (if they don't use it).
 
Other teams are experimenting with similar models, creating more ways to price, distribute and monetize inference.
 
For tokens, this creates a link with extraneous demand outside of crypto. The more people use the platform, the more valuable the credits, the more valuable the token.
 
The investment case gets stronger when usage translates into value for token holders
 
The best part is that this sector is growing fast and teams are starting to align interest with token holders through buybacks & burn, revenue distribution, and more utilities.
 
Onchain/Decentralized AI provides the opportunities for better GPU utilization, cheaper inference, new financing channels and tradable access to compute/inference.
 
All real economic problems that crypto teams are building products around them.
 
2025-26 is the year of AI infra/semiconductors
 
2027 will be the year of Onchain/Decentralized AI
